Before you make an offer, get answers to these seven questions.

1. Why is the owner selling?

2. How long has it been on the market?

3. Is the title registered and clear?

4. What are the service charges, and what do they cover?

5. Any storm or water damage?

6. If you plan to rent it out, what's the rental history?

7. What's included in the price?

The answers change what you offer. Sometimes they change whether you offer at all.

Buying property in Barbados in a seller's market begins with one fact: the seller does not need you specifically.

That is not a hostile observation. Many sellers in this market have owned for years, sometimes decades. They are not in a hurry. They have seen other buyers move through. They are calm about waiting.

What changes is not the price. It is the conversation.

Offers with extended conditions, unresolved financing, or an exploratory tone tend to receive a patient response, which usually means a slow one. The seller is simply not prioritizing them.

The buyers who do well here are not the most aggressive. They are the ones who arrive understanding the seller's actual position. They make clean offers. They ask fewer questions that reveal uncertainty. They know what they want before they say it.

We work with overseas buyers buying property in Barbados so that they understand what the market is doing before they make their first approach. In a seller's market, that understanding is not a detail. It determines who gets the conversation.

A second-home buyer is choosing where to spend a portion of the year. The property can sit empty, be let during the quieter months, and be managed from a distance. 

The brief can flex. A relocator's brief cannot. The property must work year-round. The infrastructure, connectivity, healthcare for full-time residents rather than visitors, schooling options that are fewer than buyers expect — become part of the brief in a way it never does for a second-home buyer.

The acquisition is not a lifestyle addition. It is a life change.

Most overseas buyers know which category they are in. What many do not know is that the two categories require different searches. What is excellent for one is wrong for the other.

Barbados places no restrictions on foreign property ownership. 

That is well understood. 

What is less understood is the Central Bank registration requirement — and what it actually protects.

Any foreign capital brought into Barbados to fund a property acquisition must be registered with the Exchange Control Authority of the Central Bank of Barbados.

Your attorney manages this as part of the transaction. It is a formality in the process. It is not a formality in consequence.

Correct registration at the point of purchase is what secures your right to repatriate your capital — and your gains — when you eventually exit.

Barbados applies no capital gains tax. Registration ensures that those proceeds can leave the island.

For a buyer deploying significant capital, this is not an administrative detail. It is a structural component of the acquisition.

It is one of the first things I confirm is in place.
